## Chapter 39.

<margin>1 Timothy 2:4</margin> <margin>Every man shall attend to his calling</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 7:24</margin> 1 **H**e who shall teach the Scripture should not undertake any other labor. 
2 And he who is to be taught should have nothing else to do. How can he attend to learning who must plow, and who loves to drive the oxen with whips, and occupies himself with such works, and knows nothing but to speak of oxen? 
3 He must think how he must till the fields, and must early and late give fodder to the 
4 cows. So also the carvers and carpenters who labor day and night, and carve sculpture, and use diligence to make skillful work; they must think that it becomes right, and be at it 
5 early and late so that they finish it. So a smith, who must be by his anvil, and attend to his smithy, and becomes weary from the fire, and 
6 labors himself tired before the furnace. The sound of the hammers fills his ears, and he pays attention to how he makes the work 
7 right. And he must think how he makes it ready, and be at it early and late so that 
8 he finishes it cleanly. Also a potter, who must be by his work, and turn the wheel with his feet, and must always make his work with care, and has his certain daily 
9 task. He must with his arms shape the clay into a vessel, and must bend himself tired at his feet. He must think how he glazes it finely, and early and late sweep the oven. 
10 All these trust in their handicraft. And each one busies himself that he 
11 may be skilled in his work. One cannot do without them in the city: they cannot be 
12 led anywhere else. They also cannot attend to office, nor rule in the

**50** For they are nothing but wooden, gilded, and silvered idols. Therefore it can henceforth be known to all heathens and kings that it is a deception, and they are no gods but made by human hands; and there is **51** no divinity in them. Therefore anyone can clearly perceive that they are not gods.

**52** For they do not set a King in the land, they do not give the people rain,

**53** And they do not take it upon themselves to rule or to punish, as little as the birds that fly hither and thither in the air. For

**54** when the house of the wooden, gilded, and silvered idols begins to burn, the priests run away and save themselves alone from harm. But [the idols] burn just like other beams.

**55** They can withstand neither kings nor soldiers. How shall one then consider or call them gods?

**56** The wooden, silvered, and gilded idols cannot protect themselves from thieves and robbers, for they are too strong for them,

**57** So that they rob them and strip them, taking away their gold, silver, and clothing and making off with it, and they [the idols] cannot help themselves.

**58** Therefore a king who can show his power, or a useful household vessel that is profitable in the house, or a door that guards the house, or a wooden pillar in a royal hall, is much better than such a powerless idol.

Genesis 1:16.
Baruch 3:33.

**61** And when God commands the clouds to pass over the whole world, they do what **62** their God commands. So also the fire sent from above destroys the mountains and forests, and **63** does what it is commanded. But the idols can neither nourish themselves nor do anything.

**64** Therefore one shall not consider them gods or call them so, for they can neither **65** punish nor help. Since you then know that they are not gods, do not fear them; for they can **66** neither curse nor bless kings. They **67** also cannot show any signs in the Heavens to the heathens. They cannot make light like the Sun, nor give a glow like the Moon.

<margin>
Baruch 6:14.
</margin>
**68** The irrational animals are better than they: they can at least run into a pit and protect themselves. Therefore it is in every way manifest that they are not gods; **69** therefore do not fear them. For just like a scarecrow in a garden can protect nothing, **70** so also their wooden, gilded, and silvered idols are not profitable. And just like a thornbush in the garden, upon which all kinds of birds nest, or like a dead man who lies in the grave, so are their wooden, **71** gilded, and silvered idols. Also one can perceive by this that they are not gods, for the purple clothing which they have on is eaten by moths, and they themselves at the last as well, so that everyone mocks them.

**72** Blessed is the man who is righteous and has no idols; he shall not be made a mockery.

## The First Chapter.

<margin>The power of Alexander, King of Macedonia.</margin>
Alexander the son of Philip, King of Macedonia, the first monarch from Greece, set out from the land of <term>Kittim</term><note>original: "Chitim"; refers here to Greece or the Macedonian territories.</note>, and waged great war, captured fortified cities, and slew
**2** Darius, the King of the Persians. Thereafter, he brought other kings in all lands under his rule. And
**3** he always marched forward, and conquered all lands
**4** and kingdoms. And no one
**5** dared to set themselves against him, for he had a mighty and well-equipped army.
<margin>Judith 1:8.</margin>
**6** When he had conquered the kingdoms, he became arrogant and fell into sickness. But when
**7** he noticed that he was about to die, he called his princes—who had been
<margin>Daniel 7:6.</margin>
**8** raised with him from youth—to him: And he distributed the lands among them while he was still alive. Thereafter, Alexander died, after he
**9** had reigned twelve years. After his death, the kingdom came to his princes. They took possession of the lands,
**10** and each one took his place, and they all made themselves kings. And their descendants reigned for a long time. And there were great wars between them: And everywhere in the whole world,
<margin>Daniel 8:33.</margin>
**11** much misery arose. Then, from these roots, there was born a shameful, wicked root named <term>Antiochus the Noble</term><note>original: "Antiochus de Edele"; historically known as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (the Illustrious). And this Antiochus the Noble began to reign in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the Greek Kingdom.

**18** might have both kingdoms. And he marched into Egypt well-prepared with chariots, elephants, horsemen, and many
<margin>2 Maccabees 5:1.</margin>
**19** ships, and fought with Ptolemy, the King of Egypt. But Ptolemy feared him and fled, and many Egyptians were slain.
**20** And Antiochus captured the fortified cities in Egypt, and looted great wealth there, and carried it away. But when Antiochus had thus triumphed in Egypt, and marched back home in the one hundred and
**21** forty-third year: Then he marched through Israel and came to Jerusalem with a great
<margin>2 Maccabees 5:11.</margin>
**22** multitude: And he went presumptuously into the sanctuary, and had the golden altar taken away, the lampstand, and all that belonged to it. The table where the <term>showbread</term><note>original: "toonbrooden"; the twelve loaves of bread placed weekly on a table in the Tabernacle or Temple.</note> lay, the cups, bowls, the golden basins, the veil, the crowns, and the golden decoration
<margin>2 Maccabees 5:16. Antiochus robs the temple and the city of Jerusalem.</margin>
**24** on the Temple: And he took it all, and

<column-break/>

took the silver and gold, and the precious vessels, and the hidden treasure, as much as he found, and carried it with him to his own land.
**25** And he had many people killed, and had blasphemous 
**26** commands proclaimed. And in all of Israel, wherever they lived, there was great heartache.

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous page concerning the wars of the Maccabees. It transitions from the death of King Antiochus IV to the rise of King Demetrius I and the ongoing conflict between the Jewish traditionalists led by Judas Maccabeus and the Hellenizing faction supported by the Seleucid Empire.</meta>

# Of the Maccabees.

<margin>1 Maccabees 6:14, 55</margin>
The Jews who had traveled to the lands of the Gentiles from Judea for the sake of safety <note>referring to those who sought refuge during the height of the persecution</note>, had consumed all their provisions, and the Holy ones <note>The faithful Jews</note> became very few, for they were dying of hunger. Therefore, they were forced to depart from one another and scatter into other cities.

Meanwhile, Lysias learned that Philippus—whom the King’s father Antiochus had appointed to raise the young King and manage the kingdom—had returned from Persia with the army that the King had led there, and that Philippus was taking over the government. Therefore, Lysias hurried away from Judea back to the kingdom. He spoke to the King and to the commanders: "We are suffering here from want; we have nothing to eat, and we are losing many men. Furthermore, this city <note>The Citadel or Acra in Jerusalem</note> is very strong, while we have more urgent matters to attend to at home to maintain peace in the kingdom. Let us make peace with these people and allow them to keep their Law, just as before; for they only become angry and fight because we want to take their Law away from them." This opinion pleased the King and the princes well. And the King sent to them to make a peace with them. But when they came out of the city, the King marched into it. When he saw how strong it was, he did not keep his oath, but commanded that the walls all around should be torn down again. After that, he hurried away toward Antioch. There he learned that Philippus had set himself up as King; he fought against him and took the city back.

### The Seventh Chapter.

<margin>When Demetrius 2 Maccabees 14:1</margin>
In the hundred and fifty-first year <note>Approximately 161 BCE in the Seleucid calendar</note>, Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, came from Rome back to his kingdom and captured a city by the sea with a few men, and reigned there as a King. And when he came to the capital city, Antioch, the army seized Antiochus <note>Antiochus V Eupator, the boy king</note> and Lysias, to deliver them to Demetrius. But when this was told to Demetrius, he forbade them from letting them come before his eyes. Therefore, the army killed them. Now that Demetrius held the kingdom, many godless and apostate men from Israel came to him. The most prominent among them was Alcimus, who dearly wished to become High Priest.

<margin>Antiochus and Lysias are killed.</margin>
<margin>Judas is accused before Demetrius.</margin>
These men accused Judas and their own people, saying: "Judas and his brothers have killed all those who were found to be obedient to you, or have driven them out of our land. Therefore, send someone there whom you trust, and let him see how they have destroyed us and the King’s land, and let them be punished with all their followers."

<margin>1 Maccabees 7:8</margin>
Therefore the King appointed Bacchides, his friend, who was powerful in the kingdom and whom the King trusted greatly, as a governor over the entire land on this side of the Euphrates. And he sent with him the apostate Alcimus, whom he had made High Priest, and commanded him to punish the people of Israel. They marched into the land of Judah with a large army and sent messengers to Judas and his brothers to discuss peace. And they presented themselves as if they wished to keep peace with them.

But it was nothing but deceit. Therefore, Judas did not believe them, for he saw that they were well-armed and led a large army with them. But many priests came to Alcimus and Bacchides, and many of the pious in Israel, who entrusted all their well-being to

<column-break/>

Alcimus and desired peace, saying: "Alcimus is a priest from the lineage of Aaron; he will not show us any unfaithful or malicious intent." And Alcimus promised them peace, negotiated peace, and swore an oath, saying: "We will not intentionally harm you or your friends." *As 1 Maccabees 7:31. When they now believed him in this way, he had sixty of them seized and killed them all in a single day, just as the Scripture says:

<margin>Psalm 79:2-3.</margin>
> The flesh of your Saints they have given to the beasts; they have shed their blood all around Jerusalem like water, and there was no one to bury them.

Therefore, a very great fear and terror came upon the people, who complained that there was neither faith nor loyalty in Alcimus, for he had not kept his oath. And Bacchides departed from Jerusalem and besieged Beth-zecha; he sent out and had many captured who had previously surrendered to him, and who because of the treachery had fled from him again. He had many of them killed and threw them into a large pit. Afterward, Bacchides entrusted the land to Alcimus, left soldiers with him, and he returned to the King.

And Alcimus took it upon himself to become High Priest by force, and gathered to himself all the apostates in Israel. He brought the land of Judah under him by force and plagued the people of Israel very harshly. When Judas saw that Alcimus and the apostates of Israel did much greater damage in Israel <note>than the Gentiles had done</note>, he marched again through the entire land of Judah and punished the apostates, and turned them back so that the apostates no longer dared to travel back and forth in the land. But when Alcimus saw that Judas and his people were powerful again and that he could not withstand them, he returned to the King and complained against them very harshly. Therefore, the King sent a great prince, Nicanor, there, who was very angry with the people of Israel, and commanded him to completely destroy the people of Israel.

<margin>2 Maccabees 15:1</margin>
Nicanor marched with a large army to Jerusalem and deceitfully sent messengers to Judas and his brothers, who should behave as if he only wanted to keep peace with them, saying: "We want to keep peace with one another; you and I, and I will come to you peacefully with a few people so that I may speak with you." Thus Nicanor came to Judas, and they received him, and he spoke to them under a peaceful appearance. But it was arranged that Judas should be captured there. This was made known to Judas: how Nicanor had come to him for this reason, to capture him with this deceit. Therefore, he was on his guard against him and would no longer come to him. And when Nicanor noticed that his plan had become public, he marched against Judas and held a battle with him near Caphar Salama. Afterward, Nicanor lost five thousand men, and his army had to retreat to the City of David <note>The Acra, the citadel of Jerusalem</note>. After that, Nicanor also went to the Sanctuary on Mount Zion. And the priests and the elders went out to receive him peacefully and to show him that they were making great sacrifices for the King.

<margin>2 Maccabees 14:11</margin>
But Nicanor mocked them and their religion, and blasphemed, and desecrated the sacrifice. And he swore an oath, saying: "Unless you deliver Judas and his army into my hands, I will burn this house as soon as I return successfully." And he departed in great anger. Lydia, the noblest lands, and gave them to 9 King Eumenes. The Greeks also set themselves against them with great force. > May God give the Romans and the Jews good fortune and peace by land and by water, and may He protect them from war and enemies 24 forever. If the Romans are at war in Rome or in their lands and 25 territory, the Jews shall give the Romans faithful help, according 26 as the need requires. Likewise: If war comes upon the Jews, the Romans shall help them faithfully, as the need then requires. 28 And they shall not provide the Jews' enemies with food, weapons, money, ships, or other things. This the Romans promise, and they wish to keep such a treaty faithfully 29 and without deceit.

Thus was the treaty between the Romans and the Jews 30 made. But if hereafter either party thinks of more points to add, or to change, or to remove, each party shall have the power to do so. And whatever they then add or take away shall be 31 held as valid and firm. Regarding the fact that King Demetrius acts violently against the Jews, we have written to him thus:

> Why do you plague our friends and allies? If they complain about you any more, we must protect them and will attack you by land and by water.

31 surely. Also, concerning King Demetrius using force against the Jews, we have written to him thus: 'Why do you plague our friends and allies?
32 If they complain about you any more, we must protect them and will attack you by land and by water.'"

8 to our high Priest Onias, stating that you are our brothers, as the same letter reads. And Onias received your messengers honorably and accepted the friendship and the covenant that was written of in the letter.

39 Now Tryphon <note>A military commander who sought the throne for himself</note> had determined to bring the Kingdom of Asia under his control, to set the crown upon his head, and to kill the young King Antiochus.
40 But because he feared that Jonathan would prevent him and march against him, he sought a way to capture and kill Jonathan. Therefore, he marched toward Beth-shan.
41 Then Jonathan also came there with forty thousand well-armed men.
42 But when Tryphon saw that Jonathan had a great force with him, he feared him,
43 and did not dare to act openly against him, but received him honorably and commended him to his friends, that they should treat him with respect, and gave him gifts. And he commanded his army to be as obedient to Jonathan as to himself.
44 And he said to Jonathan: "Why do you put these people to such trouble, since we have no war together?
45 Let them return home; only choose for yourself a few men to remain with you, and come with me to Ptolemais. I will give this city to you, and the other strong cities, and will entrust to you all the soldiers and officers: for I must depart again. Indeed, I have come here for this very reason. Therefore, please travel with me."

<margin>1 Maccabees 11:f</margin>

46 Jonathan believed him and let his people return home to the land of Judah, keeping only three thousand with him.
47 Of these, he sent two thousand to Galilee, but one thousand marched with him.
48 As soon as Jonathan entered the city of Ptolemais, Tryphon had the gates shut, took Jonathan prisoner, and had his men put to the sword.
49 And he sent infantry and horsemen into Galilee, onto the wide plains, to slaughter the rest of the soldiers as well.

<margin>1 Maccabees 11:g</margin>

50 But when they learned that Jonathan had been captured and killed along with his men, they encouraged one another and armed themselves for battle.
51 And they marched hastily against the enemies. But when the enemies saw that it would cost them their lives, since these men intended to defend themselves, they turned back and went away.
52 Then the people also returned home to the land of Judah in peace. And they mourned Jonathan and the others who were slain with him. And all Israel bore great grief for Jonathan.
53 And all the Heathen around them began to attack and plague the people, saying: "They no longer have a head <note>meaning a leader</note> or a protector; now we will fall upon them and destroy them, and completely wipe out their names from the earth."

<margin>Demetrius seeks help against Tryphon.</margin>
1 In the year one hundred and seventy-two, King Demetrius <note>Demetrius II Nicator</note> armed himself and marched into Media to seek help against Tryphon.

5 He also took the city of Joppa with great honor, and the harbor nearby where he could sail out by ship onto the sea to the islands.

# The Second Book of Maccabees.

<margin>23</margin> ...the whole land plundered, and a great multitude of the heathens put to flight and pursued. Furthermore, it tells of the Temple, how it was rebuilt, as is now well known everywhere, and how the city regained its freedom. <margin>24</margin> It also tells how all other laws were abolished, and only the Lord’s Law shall be kept, for He now wishes us well and is merciful. These and other matters, which Jason has written of in five books, we intend to gather here together in the briefest way. <margin>25</margin> For we see that the numbers and details are so mingled together that it is difficult for one to grasp the histories correctly, since they lie together in such a great heap. <margin>26</margin> Therefore, we have wished to arrange it so that one might read it gladly, remember it better, and that it may be profitable to everyone. <margin>27</margin> And it is true, we realize that it will be quite difficult for us to have taken this effort upon ourselves; for it requires much labor and great diligence. <margin>28</margin> Just as it is no small labor for one who prepares a meal and wishes to show friendship to their guests. <margin>29</margin> Nevertheless, we will not focus on that burden, but will gladly take this trouble upon ourselves to serve others through it. <margin>30</margin> Regarding the histories themselves, we do not wish to change them, but let them remain just as they were written before, except that we wish to draw them together more briefly. <margin>31</margin> Just as a carpenter <note>original: "Timmerman"</note>, when he builds a new house, thinks of nothing more than making the structure sound, while he leaves it to another to worry about how it shall be painted and decorated. <margin>32</margin> Thus we will also do, and let the one who originally wrote the histories worry about how he spoke all things and worked out every part with diligence. <margin>33</margin> But we will do no more than grasp the summaries in the shortest way. And we will now begin the histories, having set this down as an introduction, so that the Preface does not become larger than the entire History.

### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>Of the peaceful state of the Jews, and the glory of the Temple</margin> While they were now living again in good peace in Jerusalem, and the Law was in fine progress because the High Priest Onias was so pious and watched over it so diligently, <margin>2</margin> <margin>2 Mac. 10:39</margin> even the Kings were moved to honor the city, and sent glorious gifts into the Temple. <margin>3</margin> <margin>2 Mac 3:11. Simon, an official of the High Priest, tells Apollonius that the treasury at Jerusalem was very rich.</margin> So much so that Seleucus, the King in Asia, ordered from his own offices that all expenses needed for the sacrifices be provided. <margin>4</margin> Now there was at this time a supervisor of the Temple named Simon, a Benjamite, who was an enemy of the High Priest because he would not allow him his wantonness <note>The text suggests a disagreement over the administration of the city markets</note> in the city. <margin>5</margin> But because Onias was too powerful for him, he went to Apollonius of Coelesyria <note>original: "des Thaphenice"; this refers to the governor of the region of Coelesyria and Phoenicia</note> and told him how the treasury <note>original: "Godskiste", literally "God’s chest"</note> in Jerusalem was rich with money beyond measure, and had a vast surplus that was not needed for the sacrifices. He suggested the King might well take it for himself. <margin>7</margin> <margin>The King sends his Chamberlain to fetch the money from the treasury.</margin> When Apollonius came to the King, he told him what Simon had said regarding that money. Then the King appointed Heliodorus, his Chamberlain, and gave him a command: he was to bring that same money to him. <margin>8</margin> Heliodorus set out immediately, giving the impression that he was merely taking a journey through lower Syria and Phoenicia.

<column-break/>

<margin>9</margin> But his true intention was to fulfill the King’s command. When he arrived in Jerusalem and the High Priest had received him kindly, he told him what his Lord had commanded and why he was there, and asked if it were indeed true or not. <margin>10</margin> Then the High Priest answered: "A portion of it is kept by us in trust, belonging to widows and orphans. <margin>11</margin> The other belongs to Hyrcanus, son of Tobias, who was a very distinguished man. It is in no way as the traitor Simon has said. For there is no more than four hundred talents <note>original: "Centner", a unit of weight often translated as talents in biblical contexts</note> of silver and two hundred talents of gold. <margin>12</margin> It would be a great injustice to take it away and thus deceive those who have trusted their property to the holy Temple, which is so highly honored and protected throughout the whole world." <margin>13</margin> But Heliodorus stood by the command of the King; he insisted he must take it with him. <margin>14</margin> On a set day, he entered the Temple to divide the spoils. At this, a great lamentation arose throughout the entire city. <margin>15</margin> The priests lay in their holy vestments before the Altar and called upon God in Heaven, who gave the laws regarding deposits, that He would protect what had been placed in trusted hands. <margin>16</margin> They prayed that He would keep safe for the people the property they had deposited there in trust. But the High Priest was in such a miserable state that no one could look at him without great pity. One could see by his face how distraught he was, for he was in great anguish. <margin>17</margin> He was so terrified that he trembled from head to foot, making it easy for anyone to see how ill at ease he felt. <margin>18</margin> People ran out of their houses and gathered together to pray, seeing that the Temple was about to be brought into contempt. <margin>19</margin> The women put on sackcloth and ran through the streets. <margin>20</margin> And the young maidens, who usually did not go out in public, ran to the gates and upon the walls. Some looked out from the windows, and all raised their hands toward heaven and prayed. <margin>21</margin> It was wretched to see: the people so terrified and the High Priest so heavily burdened. <margin>22</margin> And while they were thus calling upon the Almighty God to preserve the goods of those who had deposited them in trust, <margin>23</margin> Heliodorus moved to fulfill his purpose. <margin>24</margin> As he stood by the treasury with his soldiers, the Almighty God showed a great sign, so that he and all who were with him were struck down by the power of God and fell into a state of great fear and shock. <margin>25</margin> For they saw a horse that was magnificently adorned, with a terrifying rider upon it. It charged with all its might at Heliodorus and struck at him with its front hooves. The rider on the horse wore armor made entirely of gold. <margin>26</margin> They also saw two young men who were strong, beautiful, and very well dressed. <margin>27</margin> They stood on either side of Heliodorus and struck him with all their might, so that he fell to the earth in a faint and his vision failed him. <margin>28</margin> Then they took him—the man who had so recently entered the treasury with great pride and all his soldiers—and carried him out on a litter. <margin>29</margin> His weapons and power could not help him at all. Thus, one was forced to publicly recognize the power of the Lord. <margin>30</margin> He lay there as if dead, unable to speak a word. But...

32 Now when Menelaus realized this, he thought of how he might find a favorable time to return to his former status. He stole several golden vessels from the Temple and gave them to Andronicus, and he brought others to Tyre and other surrounding cities to sell.

<margin>
How Andronicus treacherously stabbed Onias.
</margin>
33 When Onias heard of this, he went to a place of sanctuary at Daphne, which lies near Antioch, and rebuked him.
34 But Menelaus went to Andronicus alone and urged him to capture Onias. Andronicus then went to Onias and beguiled him with cunning, giving him his hand and an oath of safety so that he would leave the sanctuary to meet him. Even though Onias suspected no good from him, he came out; as soon as Andronicus had him, he stabbed him to death against all justice.
35 This did not only grieve the Jews, but it also vexed many of the Gentiles <note>original: "Heydenen," referring to non-Jewish citizens</note> that such an honorable man had been so unreasonably killed.
36 When the King had settled all matters in Cilicia and was traveling back home, the Jews in every city, and even some Gentiles, came to him and complained that the innocent Onias had been murdered.
37 And Antiochus was deeply troubled in his heart because of it. He took pity that the honorable, righteous man had perished so miserably.

<margin>
The King has Andronicus killed.
</margin>
38 He became angry with Andronicus and ordered that his purple robe and other ornaments be stripped from him, and that he be led around the entire city. Finally, he ordered him executed at the very same spot where he had stabbed Onias. Thus did God punish him according to what he deserved.

<margin>
Gen. 9 v. 6. The riot of Lysimachus against the people.
</margin>
39 But when Lysimachus, on the advice of his brother Menelaus, had stolen much from the Temple and the report of this reached the people, the multitude gathered against Lysimachus, as many golden ornaments had already disappeared.
40 Now when the multitude had gathered and become very angry, Lysimachus armed three thousand men and sought to defend himself with force, placing over them an old, cunning captain.
41 When the citizens saw this, some took up stones, some heavy clubs, and some threw ashes into their eyes, so that many of them were wounded and some were struck entirely to the earth, while the rest all fled.
42 And they caught the temple-robber <note>original: "Kerckroouer"</note> near the treasury.
43 Afterward, they brought legal charges against him. And when the King had come to Tyre,
44 they sent three members of the Council to present the case before him, so that he might pass judgment upon it.

<margin>
Ptolemy, on Menelaus's advice, persuades the King that he murdered an innocent man.
</margin>
45 But when this was reported to Menelaus, he promised Ptolemy a great sum of money if he could intercede for him with the King.
46 Then Ptolemy went alone to the King in his hall, where he was cooling himself, and persuaded the King to let Menelaus—who was the cause of all the misfortune—go free.
47 And he condemned the poor people to death, who, even before the judges <note>original: "Cateren"; contextually refers to harsh judges or Scythians, who were traditionally known for being merciless</note>, would surely have been found and declared innocent.
48 Thus were those who had handled the affairs of the people and the Temple with the utmost faithfulness, innocently murdered. This grieved some of the people of Tyre, who saw to it that they were honorably buried.

<margin>
Menelaus remains in office.
</margin>
49 But Menelaus remained in his office through the help of some powerful men at Court, who shared in his gains. And he became worse and worse, and inflicted all manner of plagues upon the citizens.

<column-break/>

1 At that same time, Antiochus made his second expedition into Egypt. But throughout the whole city, for forty days straight, riders in golden armor with long lances were seen in the sky in battle formation.
2 And people saw how they charged at one another, defending themselves with shields and spears, and how they drew their swords and shot at one another.
4 And how the golden armor gleamed, and that they wore many kinds of armor.
5 Then everyone prayed that this might not portend anything evil. But a false rumor arrived, saying that Antiochus was dead.
6 Then Jason took a thousand men with him and attacked the city before they could guard against it. And when he had climbed the walls with his men and taken the city, Menelaus fled into the citadel <note>original: "Bo2cht"</note>.
7 But Jason miserably ravaged his fellow citizens and did not consider that, since he was successful against his own friends, it was actually his own great misfortune. He let himself believe he was having success against his enemies, and not against his own citizens.
8 Yet he could not take over the government; instead, he received the reward he deserved and fled in shame back into the land of the Ammonites.
9 There he was finally accused before Aretas, the King of the Arabs, so that he had to flee from one city to another and was safe nowhere. Everyone was his enemy, as one who had fallen away from his law, and everyone cursed him as a traitor and enemy of his fatherland; and so he was driven into Egypt.
9 <note>The verse numbering repeats in the original print</note> And just as he had driven many people from their fatherland, so he himself had to die in misery in Lacedemon <note>Sparta</note>, where they were friends with one another.
10 And just as he had cast many away unburied, so he also died and no one mourned for him.
11 He not only lacked the fortune of being buried in his fatherland, but he was not even allowed a grave in foreign lands. When news of this reached the King, he thought that all of Judea would defect from him. He marched out of Egypt in a rage and took Jerusalem by force.
12 And he commanded the soldiers to slaughter <note>original: "dopen"; likely a corruption of "dooden" (to kill)</note> without any mercy everyone they found in the streets and in the houses.
13 Then they struck dead young and old, men and women, children and maidens, even the infants in the cradles.
14 So that in three days, eighty thousand were killed, forty thousand taken prisoner, and about eighty thousand were sold.
15 But Antiochus was not satisfied with this, but also attacked the holiest city on earth. And Menelaus the traitor led him into it.
16 He robbed the holy vessels with his cursed hands. And everything that other kings had given to the Temple for decoration and honor, he swept away with his sinful hands.
17 And he exalted himself greatly, not seeing that the Lord allowed such things to happen to those in the city because of their sins.
18 That was the reason God allowed the holy city to be handled so miserably. Otherwise, it would have gone for Antiochus as it did for Heliodorus, who was sent by King Seleucus to inspect the treasury and was so severely beaten for it.

46 stone. And when he had almost bled out, he took his entrails out of his body and threw them among the soldiers, and called to God, who is Lord over life and spirit, that He would give them all back to him again. # The remaining pieces of the Book of Esther from the Greek.

## The first Chapter.

<margin>The transcript of the mandate of King Artaxerxes against the Jews, given by Haman. Esth. 1. a. 1. Judit. 1. b. 8.</margin>
The letter read as follows: The great King Artaxerxes, from India to the land of the Moors <note>original: "Mozenlant," referring to Ethiopia or Cush.</note>, sends greetings to the hundred and twenty-seven Princes and their subjects. Although I am a mighty King and the greatest lord on Earth, I have not wished to exalt myself in my power, but to govern moveably, mercifully, and gently, and to preserve the dear peace in which everyone rejoices, so that every person might live quietly and pursue his business. Afterwards, I held a council with my Governors on how such might be achieved. Then Haman—my most clever, dearest, and most faithful Counselor, who is highest after the King—made known to me: that there is a people scattered in all lands that keeps special Laws, contrary to the customs of all lands and people, and always disregards the King's commands, thereby hindering peace and unity in the realm. Since we have now learned that this one people sets itself against the whole world, follows its own customs, and is disobedient to our commands, whereby they do great damage and prevent peace and unity in our Realm: Therefore we command that all those whom Haman—the chief Governor and the highest after the King, our father—can identify, be killed by the sword of their enemies, along with women and children, without any mercy, and that no one be spared. And this shall be on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month of Adar in this year, so that the disobedient may all be slain on one day, and a lasting peace be established in our Realm.

<column-break/>

But I have done it out of fear, so that I might not give the honor that belongs to my God to a man, and I will worship no one else but my God alone. And now, O Lord, King and God of Abraham, have mercy on Your people, for our enemies wish to destroy us and root out the Inheritance that You have had from the beginning. And do not despise Your little flock, which You have redeemed out of Egypt. Hear my prayer and be merciful to Your people, and change our sorrow into joy, so that we may live and praise Your name. And do not let the mouths of those who praise You be destroyed." And all Israel cried out with all their might to the Lord, for they were in mortal distress.

### The v. Chapter.

1 IN the fourth year of King Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus (of the tribe of Levi) and Ptolemy his son brought this Letter of Purim, and said: "The great King from India to Ethiopia sends his greetings to the hundred and twenty-seven Princes and their subjects. 
2 We find that there are many who misuse the princes' grace, and become 
4 bold and evil from the honor shown to them: so that they not only oppress the subjects, but even think to trample underfoot the Lord himself by whom they are exalted. 
5 And they act not only against natural Reason through ungratefulness, 
6 but are so blinded by pride that they also think that God (who sees the righteous) does not 
7 punish such unfaithfulness. They also deceive pious Princes, so that they shed innocent blood, and may bring into all misfortune those who 
8 serve faithfully and reasonably. One finds examples of this not only in Old Deeds, but also finds daily how much misfortune such unfaithful Counselors cause. Since it 
9 belongs to us to see to it that peace remains in our Realm hereafter: we might, according to the circumstances of the cases, sometimes change the commands when we find things otherwise than we were informed [thereof], and thus not proceed all too hastily. 
10 For since now Haman, the son of Hammedatha, who is from Macedonia and not of Persian blood, nor of our benevolent nature, 
11 but is a guest with us. To whom we (just as we are accustomed to do against all nations) showed all grace, and so exalted him:

12 So that we called him our Father, and he was honored by everyone as the next after the King. Yet he became so bold that he took it upon himself to bring us to the end of our Kingdom and life.

But we find that the Jews, whom that despised Scoundrel <note>original: "Schalck" – a rogue or villain.</note> wanted to have killed, are innocent, have good 
<margin>Matthew 5:45. Luke 6:35. Daniel 2:37.</margin>

1 In the second year of the great King Artaxerxes, on the first day of the 
2 month of Nisan, Mordecai—a Jew and a son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin—had a dream. He lived in the city of Susa, an honorable man 
3 who held high office in the Royal Court. <margin>2 Kings 24:14</margin> He was one of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylon, had carried away from Jerusalem with 
4 King Jeconiah, the King of Judah. <margin>Jeremiah 24:1</margin> And this was his dream: There arose 
a great noise and a roar, thundering 
5 and earthquakes upon the earth. And behold, there were two great Dragons, which came 
against each other to fight. And the 
6 noise was so great that all lands prepared themselves to fight against a 
7 holy People. And it was a day of great darkness, thick gloom, misery, and 
8 anguish, and there was great sorrow and 
9 terror upon the earth. And the holy People were greatly troubled, fearing 
their misfortune, and had already 
10 risked their lives. And they cried out to God. And after such a cry, a 
great stream of water gushed out from a small fountain. 
11 And the sun rose, and it became light; and the lowly were victorious and 
12 devoured the proud. When Mordecai awoke from the dream, he wondered what 
God intended by it. And he kept the 
13 dream in his heart and pondered it through 
the night, for he dearly wished to know 
14 what the dream signified. <margin>Interpretation of the dream.</margin> And Mordecai spoke: "God has ordained all this. I 
remember my dream, and it has happened exactly 
15 as I dreamed. The small fountain that became a great stream 
when the sun shone and the light appeared: 
16 That is Esther, <margin>Esther 2:17</margin> whom the King took as his 
lawful wife and made into a 
17 Queen. The two Dragons are Haman and I. One signifies the Heathens, who came together to 
completely destroy the name 
18 of the Jews. The other signifies my people Israel, who cried out to the Lord, 
19 and the Lord helped his people and delivered us from this misfortune. <margin>Daniel 6:27</margin> He performs great signs and wonders among the Heathens. 
20 <margin>God delivers his people when they are at their weakest, and punishes the heathens when they are at their boldest.</margin> For he has always maintained a distinction between his people and the Heathens. 
21 And when the time came that the Heathens were at their boldest, and we were at our 
weakest, and God 
wished to judge: then he 

<column-break/>

remembered his people and gave his inheritance the 
22 victory. And these days shall be observed in the month of Adar, on the fourteenth 
and fifteenth day of the same month, with 
all joy and great diligence 
when the people gather together. 
23 And they shall be kept thus eternally among the people of Israel."

Lord Almighty *God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of their righteous seed: *You who made Heaven and Earth, with all that is therein. *And have sealed the sea with your commandments, and have shut up the deep, and sealed it, to the honor of your fearful and glorious Name: So that everyone must tremble before you, <margin>Isaiah 2:10</margin> <margin>5</margin> *and fear your great power, for your <margin>Exodus 20:6</margin> wrath is unbearable, with which you threaten sinners: But *unspeakable is the mercy of your promises: <margin>Exodus 34:6 Psalm 86:5</margin> for you are the Lord, the Most High over the whole Earth, *long-suffering, of great goodness, and very merciful, and <margin>Luke 24:46 Acts 2:38.</margin> do not punish people gladly, and have promised according to your goodness, *repentance for the forgiveness of sins. ### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>Then the wisdom of the youths, concerning what is strongest.</margin>
1 Then the second began to speak, who had said that the King was the strongest, and said: O you men, are not those men the strongest and most prominent who have dominion over land and sea, and all that is in the sea and on the earth?
2 So the King is indeed lord over all these things, and rules over them all, and whatever he commands, that is done.
3 If he tells his sons <note>original: "zonen", here referring to his subjects or soldiers</note> to go into war, so they go, and level mountains, walls, and towers.
4 They are killed, and they also kill, and they do not transgress the word of the King.
5 If they are victorious, they bring all the spoil to the King. Likewise also the others who do not go to war, but till the earth,
6 when they reap, they bring tribute to the King. And he is the only King; if he commands to kill, they kill:
7 If he commands to spare, they spare: If he bids them strike, they strike:
8 If he bids them lay waste, they lay waste: If he bids them build, they build:
9 If he bids them break down, they break down: If he bids them plant, they plant:
10 The common people and the rulers are obedient to him, and yet above all that, the King sits down, eats, drinks, and sleeps:
11 For those who guard around the King and none of them depart, but they must be obedient to the King.
12 O you men, how can he not far excel others, to whom men are so obedient? And when he had spoken this, he held his peace.

1 Then Esdras stood up from the court of the Temple outside, and went away into the sleeping chamber of Jonathan the son of Masabi.

<meta>This page continues the text of 2 Esdras (4 Ezra). On the previous page, the prophet Ezra was fasting and praying in a field called Ardath. He encountered a woman mourning the death of her only son on his wedding night. Ezra rebuked her, telling her she should mourn for the city of Zion instead of her individual loss. As he spoke, the woman was suddenly transformed into a great, shining city.</meta>

### The 11th Chapter.

Then I saw *a dream. And from the other sea an **Eagle** <note>original: Arent</note> flew up, which had twelve wings and three heads; he stretched his wings over all the earth, and all the winds blew upon them, and they were gathered together.
3 From the feathers grew other small feathers. And the heads were resting; the middle head was larger than the others, yet it also rested with the others. Furthermore I saw that the Eagle flew with his wings and reigned upon the earth and over all who dwelt upon the earth. All things under heaven were subject to him; no one was rebellious to him, no, not one creature on the face of the earth. Then I saw how the Eagle stood up on his claws and gave a cry with his feathers, and a voice that sounded thus: You shall not all watch together; each one shall sleep in his place and watch for a time. But the heads shall be preserved until the last. But I saw that the voice did not come out of his heads, but from the middle of his body. The other feathers that were opposite to it, I counted; there were eight of them. And from the right side a feather stood up and reigned over all the earth. And it happened that when it had reigned, its end came, and its place appeared no more. Then the next one stood up and reigned, and had a long time. And when it had reigned, its end also came like the one before it, so that it appeared nowhere anymore. Then a voice came to it and said: Hear, you who have held the earth for so long, this I say to you, that you cease to be; no one shall hold your time after you, no, not even half the time. Then the third rose up and reigned like the previous ones, and was also no more. Thus it went with all the others one after another, so that each one reigned and was no more. Then I spoke, and behold: In that time the following feathers shall be raised up on the right side, so that they also might reign, and some among those reigned also. But immediately they were seen no more. For some of them were raised up, yet they did not reign. After this I saw that the twelve wings were no longer there, nor the two small wings. And there was nothing more on the body of the Eagle except two heads that rested and six small feathers. Then I saw further that the six small feathers were divided in two, and remained under the head that was on the right side; for the four remained in their place. Then I saw that those under the wings undertook to raise themselves up and to reign. Then one was raised up, but as quickly it was nowhere more. And the others were gone faster than the first. Then the two also thought within themselves to reign. And as they thought this, one of the resting heads awoke, namely the large and the middle one. And then I saw that two heads were united with it. And that head turned with those who were with it and devoured the two lower wings that wanted to have reigned. But that head terrified the whole earth and reigned on the earth over those who dwelt on the earth with much labor, and had

<summary>In this passage, Ezra receives the interpretation of his vision of the Messiah and is then commanded by God to miraculously rewrite the Holy Scriptures, which had been lost when the Law was burned. Drinking a cup of "fiery water," Ezra is inspired to dictate 204 books over forty days to five scribes.</summary>

<summary>This page describes a series of divine judgments including famine, war, and desolation sent upon the nations of Babylon, Asia, Egypt, and Syria. It concludes with an exhortation for the faithful to live as "pilgrims" on earth, detached from worldly possessions and status as the end approaches.</summary>

212 Thus those who were previously despised and scorned, and near death—indeed, many who were as if already in the lamentable mourning of death—rejoiced in a joyful and blessed feast; they gathered and, in the places that had previously appeared to them as graves, they distributed portions among themselves in companies <note>original: "Centen wijse," likely a translation of the Greek "symposia," referring to groups or mess-parties.</note> with joy, and they arranged everything well:
213 They took up their songs (which they used in the land of their fathers), and therewith praised their God, their Savior and Wonder-worker; they were released from all mourning and sadness, and they performed a dance as a sign of their joy.
214 Likewise, the King held a great banquet and meal, and as a man invited to it, he graciously acknowledged God in Heaven and praised God richly, that He had so unexpectedly restrained him against his own intention.
215 Those who had previously considered the Jews as food for the birds and the beasts, and had joyfully set them under the Ban <note>A sentence of destruction or excommunication.</note>, felt regret and were ashamed; they were dishonorably destroyed by the unforeseen divine wrath.
216 And the Jews (as was said before) celebrated such a right with the joyful meal, with thanksgiving and songs of praise; they therefore established a common law in all their dwellings for all time, to spend the aforementioned day in joy—and that not for the sake of gluttony or drinking, but for the sake of the salvation and the help that their God had shown them.
217 Furthermore, when they had finished this joyful and high festival, they went to the King and requested leave to return to their fatherland.

## Of the Maccabees

<margin>The King gives the Jews a letter of safe-conduct to return to their Land again.</margin>
221 And what they stood in need of was given and provided to them by the King until the fourteenth day, during which time they held discussions together regarding their deliverance.

222 The King also gave them his word and invited them; therewith he drafted this letter for them, or wrote a letter of safe-conduct to all governors and chieftains in all cities, which letter was composed in a magnanimous and fiery spirit, according to the following meaning and form.

<margin>The King has the Jews released.</margin>
222 King Ptolemy Philopator wishes all Superiors and Prominent men in Egypt, and all prominent Officers, joy and health.

223 We and our sons are healthy and prosper, through the great God, who successfully carries out all our dealings according to all our will and wish.

224 Furthermore, know that some of my untrustworthy friends have frequently approached us and have often caused us to attempt to forge together <note>The Dutch "smaden" or "smeden" here implies binding or plotting against them.</note> all the Jews who are settled throughout my Kingdom.

225 And to punish them with a new penalty for disobedience, whereby they claimed our affairs would certainly not proceed with gravity nor come to a right peaceful state, and thus we would have neither peace nor rest until their enmity (with which they plotted against us) had run its course.

<margin>Of the joyful banquet and feast of the Jews.</margin>
226 They [the advisors] treated them as nothing other than their own property—yea, tortured them like traitors—and undertook to kill them without any distinction or recognized leave, and allowed a more tyrannical judgment to pass over them than the seven plagues <note>original: "Septen plagen"; likely a reference to the biblical plagues of Egypt, though the text specifies "seven."</note>.

227 For which reason we have diligently threatened them, and out of mercy (seeing as we are benevolent and mild-tempered toward all the world), we have preserved their lives.

<margin>John 10:11</margin>
228 And as we recognized the Heavenly God, who has stood by the Jews, that He fought for them just as a father for his child, also seeing their steadfast friendship and good-willed submission with which they have honored us and our ancestors.

229 So we have (according to the circumstances of the matter) released them all again in a proper manner, and have arranged that everyone may move back to his own, and that in no place where he dwells shall harm befall him, nor should he be despised on account of any past matters.

<margin>Jeremiah 30:16; Zechariah 2:8</margin>
230 For you shall know that if we were to inflict any evil against them contrary to right, or burden them in any way, we would have not a man, but God Himself who has power over all, standing against us as an unyielding enemy, whose vengeance we can in no way escape nor flee from. God preserve your health.

<margin>The Jews request of the King that they may punish the apostates. 2 Maccabees 1:67.</margin>
231 When they had now received this epistle, they did not open it immediately upon the departure of the Jews, but they petitioned the King that he would grant them leave to punish the Jews who had willfully and unforced abandoned the holy God and stepped away from His law:

232 For it is well to be suspected that those who have transgressed the divine law solely for the sake of the belly <note>That is, for material gain or physical survival.</note> would never be faithful to the King, nor ever be obedient to his commands.

<column-break/>

233 When the King specifically understood and noticed that they were presenting the truth to him, he gave them his word, and on account of those things (as explained above) gave them full authority, so that they should kill all those who had become apostate from the divine Law, throughout the entire Kingdom, without pity or mercy, according to the King's previously issued mandate, following a broader command given upon the King's inquiry.

234 For this they praised and thanked the King (as was fitting), likewise their Priests with all the congregation sang Hallelujah—that is, Praise be to God <note>original: "Haleluia"</note>—and thus they journeyed away with joy.

235 And on the way, they punished all those among them who had defiled themselves, and after many shames they inflicted upon them, they killed them; so that in one day they killed more than three hundred men (who had strayed against the Law), held a celebration, and cast out the wicked from among them.

236 But those who had clung fast to God unto death remained everywhere blessed and upright; they were crowned with fragrant wreaths upon their heads and moved out of the city with joy and a cheerful sound, thanking the God of their fathers, the holy protector of Israel.

237 And after they came to Ptolemais (which was called "Rose-bearing" <note>original: "Roosen vzuchtich"</note> because of the characteristics of the place), there were some appointed sea-ships and galleys waiting for them for seven days; so they held a very great and magnificent banquet there as a memorial of their deliverance and departure, for which the King gave enough of every necessity that each required until he reached home.

238 And when they had traveled away in peace and with laudable thanksgiving, they resolved there (as before) to grace those other days with joy until the completion of their pilgrimage.

239 Whereby they erected a memorial column and vowed and confirmed a promise to God.

240 Thus they passed through, unburdened, unhurt, free, secure, and joyfully over water and over land, by command of the King, each into his own property.

241 And henceforth they had great power against those who hated them.

242 And they were thus displaced or burdened by no one on account of their goods, but brought everything home, free and clear, from the exile.

243 Even those who had taken anything from them restored it with great concern.

244 And all this was wrought by the Most High God, who did great wonders in their deliverance.

245 To the blessed, highly-praised Savior of Israel, be Glory and Praise from now unto Eternity, Amen.

<summary>This page contains a significant portion of Jesus's Sermon on the Mount, where he reinterprets the Mosaic Law to emphasize inner intent over outward compliance. It includes instructions on reconciliation, personal morality, the Lord's Prayer, and the warning against serving wealth (Mammon).</summary>

# Jesus sends his Apostles. Gospel.

...and heal all kinds of sicknesses and all kinds of infirmities. <margin>Names of the Apostles.</margin> 2 The names of the twelve Apostles are these: The first, Simon, called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
3 Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the Tax Collector; James the son of Alphaeus;
4 Lebbaeus, surnamed Thaddaeus; Simon of Cana, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
5 These twelve Jesus sent out, and commanded them, and spoke: "Do not go on the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into a city of the Samaritans.
6 But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
7 <margin>The Apostles are sent to the house of Israel. Acts 3:19; Mark 6:8-9; Luke 9:3.</margin> Go, and preach, and say: 'The Kingdom of Heaven has come near.'
8 Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out the demons. Freely you have received, freely give.
9 You shall have no gold, nor silver, nor copper in your belts,
10 <margin>Luke 10:17; 1 Timothy 5:18; Mark 6:10.</margin> Nor a bag for the journey, nor two coats, nor shoes, nor a staff: For a worker is worthy of his food.
11 But into whatever City or Village you enter, inquire if anyone there is worthy. And stay with them until you depart from there.
12 And when you enter a house, greet it:
13 And if that house is worthy, let your peace come upon it: But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
14 <margin>Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5; Acts 13:51.</margin> And whoever will not receive you, nor hear your words, depart out of that house or city, and shake the dust off your feet.
15 <margin>Those who do not receive Christ will not be saved by him. <note>Original "blost" is an archaic form related to "verlost," meaning saved or delivered.</note></margin> Truly I say to you: It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah <note>Two biblical cities destroyed by fire for their wickedness; used here as a benchmark for judgment.</note> in the day of judgment, than for such a city.

17 <margin>The Cross and suffering. Mark 13:9; Luke 21:11; John 16:2; Revelation 2:10.</margin> But beware of men, for they will deliver you up to their councils, and they will scourge you in their schools <note>Meaning synagogues or places of assembly/instruction.</note>.
18 And you shall be led before Princes and Kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.

20 what you shall speak. For it is not you who speaks, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks through you.
21 <margin>Micah 7:6; 4 Esdras 9:5.</margin> Brother shall deliver up brother to death, and the Father the Son, and children shall rise up against their parents and help put them to death.
22 And you must be hated by everyone for my Name’s sake.
23 <margin>Matthew 24:13. The benefit of perseverance. Matthew 4:12; Acts 8:1; Luke 6:49; John 13:16.</margin> But whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved. But when they persecute you in one city, flee to another: Truly I say to you: You shall not finish the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes.
24 <margin>The Disciple is not above his master.</margin> The Disciple is not above his Master, nor the Servant above the Lord.
25 <margin>Matthew 12:24.</margin> It is enough for the Disciple to be like his Master, and the Servant like his Lord. If they have called the Master of the house Beelzebub <note>A name used for the prince of demons; literally "Lord of the Flies."</note>, how much more shall

for a penny? Yet not one of them falls to the earth without your father.

33 But whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my heavenly Father.

1 And it happened, when Jesus had finished giving these commands to his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and to preach in their cities.
2 And when John, being in prison, heard of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples, and had them say to him:
3 "Are you the one who is to come, or should we wait for another?"
4 Jesus answered and spoke to them: "Go and tell John again what you see and hear:
5 The blind see, and the lame walk; the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear; the dead rise up, and the Gospel is preached to the poor.
6 And blessed is he who is not offended by me."
7 As they departed, Jesus began to speak to the people concerning John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? Did you want to see a reed shaken to and fro by the wind?
8 Or what did you go out to see? Did you want to see a man in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in Kings' houses.
9 Or what did you go out to see? Did you want to see a Prophet? Yes, I say to you, one who is even more than a Prophet.
10 For this is he of whom it is written: 'Behold, I send my Messenger <note>The original Dutch uses "Enghel" (Angel), from the Greek "angelos," which means messenger.</note> before you, who shall prepare your way before you.'
11 Truly I say to you: Among all those born of women, no one has arisen who is greater than John the Baptist. But he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he.
12 But from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who do violence take it by force.
13 For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.
14 And if you will receive it: He is Elijah, who was to come.
15 He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

34 Now when the time of the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the Vineyard Workers,

### The 22nd Chapter.

<margin>Luke 14.b.16. Of those invited to the wedding who refused to come.</margin>
1 And Jesus answered, and spoke again by parables to them, and said:
2 "The Kingdom of Heaven is like a King, who made a Wedding for his son."
<margin>Revelation 19.b.9.</margin>
3 And sent his servants out, to call the guests to the Wedding. And they would not come.
<margin>Isaiah 25.b.6</margin>
4 Again he sent other servants out, and said: "Tell the guests: See, I have prepared my meal, my oxen and my fatted cattle are slaughtered, and everything is ready, come to the Wedding."
5 But they disregarded it, and went away, one to his Field, the other to his business.
6 But some seized his servants, insulted and killed them. When the King heard that,
7 he was angry, and sent out his Army, and destroyed these Murderers, and set their city on fire.
8 Then he said to his servants: "The Wedding is indeed ready, but the guests were not
9 worthy. Go therefore out into the streets,
10 and invite to the Wedding whoever you find." And the servants went out into the streets, and brought together everyone they found, bad and good, and the tables were all full. Then the King came
11 in to see the guests. And he saw there a man, who did not have a Wedding garment on.
<margin>Among the invited, one is found without a wedding garment.</margin>
12 And he spoke to him: "Friend, how did you come in here and yet have no Wedding garment on?"

15 Then the Pharisees went away, and took counsel, how they might trap him in his
16 speech. And they sent to him their disciples, with Herod's servants, and said: "Master, we know that you are true, and teach the way of God rightly, and you do not care for anyone, for you do not regard the appearance of men.
17 Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it right that one should give tribute <note>original: "chijns," a tax or census payment</note> to Caesar, or not?"
18 But when Jesus noticed their wickedness, he said: "You hypocrites, why do you tempt me?
19 Show me the tribute coin." And they reached him
20 a penny <note>original: "penninc," referring to the Roman denarius</note>. And he said to them: "Whose is this image and the inscription?"
21 They said to him: "Caesar's." Then he said to them: "So give to Caesar what is Caesar's: and
22 to God, what is God's." When they heard that, they marveled, and left him, and went
23 away. The same day, the Sadducees came to him, who hold that there is no resurrection, and asked him,
24 And said: "Master, Moses said, if a man dies and has no children, then his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed for his brother.
25 Now there were seven brothers with us; the first married, and died. And because he had no seed, he left his wife to his brother.
26 Likewise the second,
27 and the third, even unto the seven.
28 Lastly, after them all, the wife died also.
29 Now in the resurrection, whose wife shall she be among the seven? For they all had her."
30 But Jesus answered, and said to them: "You err, and do not know the Scriptures, nor the power
31 of God. In the resurrection they shall not marry, nor be given in marriage, but they are like the Angels of God in
32 Heaven. But have you not read concerning the resurrection of the dead, what was said to you by God, where he says: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?
33 But God is not a God of the dead, but of the living." And when the people heard that,
34 they were astonished at his teaching. But when the Pharisees heard that he had stopped the mouth of the Sadducees, they gathered
35 together. And one among them, a Scribe <note>original: "Schriftgheleerde," one learned in the Law of Moses</note>, tempted him, and said: "Master,
36 which is the foremost commandment in the law?"
37 Jesus said to him: "You shall love God your Lord, with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind. This is the
38 foremost and the greatest commandment.
39 The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
40 On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets."
41 Now while the Pharisees were together, Jesus asked them, and said:
42 "What do you think of Christ, whose son is he?"
43 They said: "David's." He said to them: "How then? Where he says: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,
44 until I make your enemies a footstool
45 for your feet. If David then calls him a Lord, how is he then his son?" And no one
46 could answer him a word. And no one dared ask him any more from that day on.

3 "There is the voice of a Preacher in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his footpaths straight." John was in the wilderness baptizing and preached the baptism of repentance <note>original: "boete"; can mean penance or repentance</note> for the forgiveness of sins.

14 But after John was delivered up, Jesus came into Galilee and preached the Gospel of the kingdom of God,

20 And immediately he called them. And they left their father Zebedee in the Ship with the hired servants and followed him.

21 And they went to Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath, he went into the school <note>original: "schole"; used here to mean the synagogue</note> and taught.

22 And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught with authority and not as the Scribes.

23 And there was a man in their synagogue possessed by an unclean spirit, who cried out,

26 And the unclean spirit tore him, and cried loudly, and came out of him.

27 And they were all so amazed that they questioned among themselves and spoke: "What is this? What kind of new teaching is this? He commands the unclean spirits with authority, and they obey him."

28 And his fame was quickly spread throughout the region of Galilee.

29 And they went immediately out of the synagogue and came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.

30 And Simon’s mother-in-law lay sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.

31 And he stepped toward her, and raised her up, holding her by the hand; and the fever left her immediately, and she served them.

32 And in the evening, when the Sun had gone down, they brought all kinds of sick and possessed people to him.

33 And the whole city gathered at the door.

34 And he helped many sick people who were burdened with many kinds of diseases, and drove out many devils, and did not let the devils speak, because they knew him.

35 And in the morning he stood up before daybreak and went out. And Jesus went into a deserted place and prayed there.

36 And Peter, with those who were with him, followed him quickly.

37 And when they found him, they spoke to him: "Every man seeks you."

38 And he spoke to them: "Let us go into the next towns, so that I may preach there also, for that is why I have come."

39 And he preached in their synagogues in all of Galilee and drove out the devils.

40 And there came a leprous man to him, who begged him, kneeled before him, and spoke to him: "If you will, you are well able to cleanse me."

41 And Jesus had compassion on him, and he reached out his hand, touched him, and spoke: "I will do it; be cleansed."

42 And as he spoke thus, the leprosy left him immediately, and he became clean.

43 And Jesus warned him and sent him away immediately.

### Chapter 10.

1 <margin>A</margin> **I**n the fifteenth year of the reign of Emperor Tiberius / when Pontius Pilate was governor in Judea / and Herod was a Tetrarch <note><term>Tetrarch</term>: A ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom or province.</note> in Galilee / and his brother Philip a Tetrarch in Iturea / and in the region of Trachonitis / and Lysanias a Tetrarch of Abilene /
2 When Annas and Caiaphas were high priests / then the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

5 Every valley shall be filled / and every mountain and hill shall be brought low: And what is crooked / shall be made straight: And what is uneven / shall be made a smooth way.
6 And all flesh shall see the Savior of God.

9 The axe is already laid to the root of the trees: Which tree brings forth no good fruit / it is cut down and thrown into the fire.
10 And the people asked him / saying: What shall we do then?
11 He answered / and said to them: He who has two coats <note>original: "rocken," referring to tunics or undergarments</note> / let him give to him / who has none: And he who has food / let him do likewise.
12 The tax collectors <note><term>Tollenaers</term>: Publicans or tax collectors, often despised in biblical times for their cooperation with Roman authorities.</note> also came / to be baptized / and said to him: Master / what shall we do then?
13 He said to them: Demand no more / than what is appointed.

### The 19th Chapter.

<summary>This page contains Jesus' teachings on the suddenness of his return, comparing it to the days of Noah and Lot, followed by parables on persistent prayer (the Unjust Judge) and humility (the Pharisee and the Tax Collector). It also records the encounter with the rich young ruler and the healing of a blind man near Jericho.</summary>

<margin>Of Zacchaeus</margin> 1 And he entered and passed through Jericho.
2 <margin>a</margin> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, who was a chief among the tax collectors <note>original: "Tollenaren", officials who collected taxes for the Roman Empire, often seen as traitors by fellow Jews</note>, and he was rich.
3 And he sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, for he was small of stature.
4 And he ran ahead and climbed up into a mulberry tree <note>original: "Moerbesienboom"; while often translated as a sycamore in English Bibles, the Dutch text specifies a mulberry</note>, so that he might see him, for he was to pass that way.
5 And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him: Zacchaeus, come down quickly, for today I must stay at your house.
6 And he came down quickly, and received him with joy.
7 <margin>Acts 16:34</margin> When they saw that, they all murmured, saying that he had gone to be a guest with a man who is a sinner.
8 <margin>An example of true repentance.</margin> But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have cheated anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.
9 And Jesus said to him: Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham.
10 <margin>Matthew 15:24</margin> For the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.
11 While they were listening to these things, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem, and they thought that the kingdom of God would appear immediately. And he spoke:
12 <margin>Matthew 25:14; Mark 13:34</margin> A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and then return.
13 <margin>A parable of a lord who gave his servants pounds.</margin> He called ten of his servants and gave them ten pounds <term>pounds: "pont", referring to a "mina," a unit of currency worth about three months' wages</term>, and said to them: Do business until I come back.
14 <margin>b</margin> But his citizens hated him and sent a message after him, saying: We do not want this man to reign over us.
15 And it happened that when he returned, having received the kingdom, he commanded these servants to be called to him, to whom he had given the money, so that he might know what every man had gained by trading.
16 <margin>Matthew 25:20. The first.</margin> Then came the first, saying: Lord, your pound has gained ten pounds.
17 And he said to him: Well done, you good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.
18 <margin>The second.</margin> The second came and said: Lord, your pound has yielded five pounds.
19 <margin>Gained</margin> To him he also spoke: And you shall be over five cities.
20 <margin>The third, who was punished for his laziness.</margin> And the third came and said: Lord, behold, here is your pound, which I have kept hidden in a handkerchief <note>original: "Sweetdoeck", literally a "sweat-cloth"</note>.
21 For I feared you, because you are a harsh man; you take up what you did not lay down, and reap what you did not sow.
22 <margin>2 Samuel 1:16; Matthew 12:37</margin> He said to him: Out of your own mouth I will judge you, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow.
23 <margin>Mark 4:24; Luke 8:18.</margin> Why then did you not give my money to the bank? Then when I came, I might have required it with interest.
24 <margin>c</margin> And he said to those who stood by: Take the pound from him, and give it to him who has ten pounds.
25 And they said to him: Lord, he already has ten pounds.
26 <margin>Matthew 13:12.</margin> I say to you: To everyone who has shall be given; but from him who has not, even that which he has shall be taken away.
27 But those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay them before me.
28 And when he had said this, he went on ahead, traveling up to Jerusalem.
29 <margin>Matthew 21:1; Mark 11:1.</margin> And it happened, when he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, and came to the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,
30 <margin>Jesus sent two of his disciples for a donkey</margin> Saying: Go into the village opposite you; and as you enter it, you shall find a colt <note>original: "Duelen", an archaic term for a young donkey</note> tied,

<column-break/>

on which no man has ever sat; untie it and bring it here.
31 And if anyone asks you why you are untying it, say this to him: The Lord has need of it.
32 And those who were sent went their way and found it just as he had said to them.
33 And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: Why are you untying the colt?
34 And they said: The Lord has need of it.
35 And they brought it to Jesus; and they threw their garments on the colt and set Jesus upon it.

42 If only you had known, even you, at least in this your day, the things which belong to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.

### The 7th Chapter.

Then the high priest spoke: "Is this so?"
2 And he said: "Dear brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran <note>original: "Charam"</note>,
3 And spoke to him: 'Go out from your country and from your kindred, and come into a land which I will show you.'
4 Then he went out of the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And from there, after his father was dead, He brought him over into this land where you now live.
5 And He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth, yet He promised him: He would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring after him, when he yet had no child.
6 But God spoke thus: 'That his offspring shall be a stranger in a foreign land, and they shall make them bondservants and treat them ill for four hundred years.
7 And the nation whom they shall serve, I will judge,' says God. 'And after that they shall come out and serve me in this place.'
8 And He gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so he begat Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat the twelve Patriarchs <note>original: "Aertsvaderen"</note>.
9 And the Patriarchs, being jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt.
10 But God was with him, and delivered him out of all his troubles, and gave him grace and wisdom before King Pharaoh in Egypt, who appointed him as lord over Egypt and over his whole house.
11 And there came a famine over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great distress, and our fathers found no sustenance.
12 But when Jacob heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent our fathers there the first time.
13 And at the second time, Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s lineage became known to Pharaoh.
14 And Joseph sent and called his father Jacob and all his kindred, seventy-five souls.
15 And Jacob went down into Egypt and died, he and our fathers.
16 And they were carried over to Shechem <note>original: "Sichem"</note> and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of money from the children of Hamor at Shechem.
17 But when the time of the promise drew near, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
18 Until another King arose who did not know Joseph.
19 This man dealt craftily with our race and mistreated our fathers, so that they had to cast out their young children, so that they might not live.
20 At that time Moses was born, and was a fine child before God, and was nourished for three months in his father’s house.
21 And when he was cast out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son.

He went in to them; and because he was of the same craft, he stayed with them and worked. (They were tentmakers by trade <note>original: "Tapeetmakers," literally tapestry or carpet makers, but traditionally translated as tentmakers in this context.</note>). It happened while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul walked through the upper regions and came to Ephesus, and found some disciples, to whom he said: "Have you received the Holy Spirit since you became believers?" -> The 20th Chapter. <-

1 When the uproar had ceased, Paul called the disciples to him, bid them farewell, and departed to travel into Macedonia.
